core: Definition of heuristic evaluation: experts review an interface against a checklist of usability principles (working definition, attributed to Jakob Nielsen)
Nielsen's ten usability heuristics, each with a one-line plain meaning
The process: a small team of evaluators inspects independently, then findings are combined and discussed
Severity ratings: problems are rated (frequency, impact, persistence; 0-4 scale) so teams fix the worst first
The distinction from usability testing: expert review vs. observation of real users; the two complement each other
supporting: Heuristics are broad rules of thumb, not specific guidelines or laws
Why 3-5 independent evaluators beat one (any single expert misses issues)
Heuristic evaluation is fast and inexpensive because no participants are needed; useful early in design and on limited budgets
Violations are candidate problems: context matters, and real users confirm which issues actually matter
outOfScope: Accessibility and WCAG (sibling topics: ux-ui-design:foundations:accessibility, wcag-basics)
Evaluating specific real products as good or bad design

claims.claim: Heuristic evaluation is a usability inspection method in which evaluators judge an interface against a set of guidelines (heuristics) that make systems easy to use; it does not involve testing with users.
The most widely used checklist is Jakob Nielsen's set of ten usability heuristics, published in 1994 and refined from earlier heuristics Nielsen developed with Rolf Molich (1990).

The ten heuristics are: visibility of system status; match between the system and the real world; user control and freedom; consistency and standards; error prevention; recognition rather than recall; flexibility and efficiency of use; aesthetic and minimalist design; help users recognize, diagnose, and recover from errors; help and documentation.
The heuristics are called heuristics because they are broad rules of thumb, not specific usability guidelines; they are guidelines rather than laws, and context can justify exceptions.

Heuristic evaluation works best with a group: ideally three to five people should independently evaluate the same interface, because each individual, however expert, is likely to miss some usability issues.

The standard process has two phases: each evaluator first becomes familiar with the product, then walks through it again looking for violations of the heuristics and recording issues; afterwards the team consolidates the findings, discusses agreements and disagreements, and prioritizes.

Severity of a usability problem combines three factors: frequency (common or rare), impact (easy or difficult to overcome), and persistence (one-time or repeatedly bothersome); a common rating scale runs 0 (not a usability problem) to 4 (usability catastrophe), with 1 cosmetic, 2 minor, 3 major.
Heuristic evaluation is fast and inexpensive compared with methods involving real users, which makes it useful early in the design process and for stretching a limited UX research budget.

Heuristic evaluation cannot replace user research or usability testing: expert judgments are assumptions about good usability, evaluations can produce false alarms, and only observing real users confirms which problems actually matter.

Heuristic evaluation and usability testing find different kinds of problems and work well together; for example, an evaluation before a usability test can identify which design elements the test should focus on.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Does a heuristic violation always mean the design has a real usability problem?
positions: Nielsen Norman Group: a violation is a signal, not a verdict. The team's own example is a hamburger menu, which violates the recognition-rather-than-recall heuristic but is often the right choice on mobile; 'heuristics are guidelines, not laws.'

Interaction Design Foundation: heuristic evaluation is based on assumptions about what good usability is, and it can produce false alarms; one reported comparative study found many problems flagged by heuristic evaluators were not genuine problems for real users (IxDF reports 43% of flagged issues were not actual problems and that evaluators identified a minority of the genuine problems that usability testing found).
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson frames heuristic findings as candidate problems that must be confirmed with real users and weighed in context; it does not reproduce the specific study percentages.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Is heuristic evaluation a replacement for or a complement to usability testing?
positions: Both sources agree expert review cannot replace testing with real users; NN/g stresses that UX design is highly contextual and that evaluations complement research.
Some practitioners describe heuristic evaluation as a cheap substitute when budgets cannot support testing; both NN/g and IxDF explicitly reject using it that way.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson teaches the complement framing: heuristics find likely problems, usability testing confirms them.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The machine-generated draft's boilerplate (none of it survived; the phase-2 draft for this topic was generic and contained no specific verifiable claims to carry over).
correctionsNeeded: Attributed the ten heuristics precisely: refined and published by Jakob Nielsen (1994), with roots in the 1990 Nielsen-Molich heuristics.
Kept severity factors to frequency, impact, and persistence (plus market impact as an additional consideration), per Nielsen's severity article.
Used the current NN/g wording for heuristic names (e.g., 'Consistency and Standards', 'Recognition Rather than Recall').
rightsIssues: All four sources are reference-only: NN/g articles are public but copyrighted; the IxDF topic page carries a CC BY-SA 4.0 mark on some materials, but no source wording was reproduced, so REFERENCE_ONLY applies throughout.

sourceRecords.title: 10 Usability Heuristics for User Interface Design
sourceRecords.notes: Jakob Nielsen's canonical list of the ten usability heuristics with plain-language descriptions, first published 1994 and last reviewed January 2024. Read live; used for the names of the ten heuristics, the 'broad rules of thumb, not specific guidelines' framing, and the one-line meanings.

sourceRecords.title: Heuristic Evaluations: How to Conduct
sourceRecords.notes: Kate Moran and Kelley Gordon's step-by-step guide (2023): definition of the method, 3-5 independent evaluators, two-pass review (familiarization, then issue-hunting), consolidation of findings, exceptions to heuristics, and the statement that heuristic evaluations cannot replace user research. Read live; used for the process description and the complement framing.

sourceRecords.notes: Jakob Nielsen (1994) on severity: the three factors (frequency, impact, persistence, with market impact as an extra consideration) and the 0-4 rating scale from cosmetic to usability catastrophe. Read live; used for the severity section.
